items.body: After several records examining language (Pause/Stutter/Uh/Repeat), mutation (Mutate), liturgical memory (Ison), and the algorithmic logic of social media (Kitbashing), Abadir arrives at what feels like the conceptual centre of his work. The Primitivist is not simply a new collection of club tracks but a declaration of intent, rejecting electronic music’s enduring fixation with futurism in favour of a deeper engagement with the present and with the musical traditions that continue to shape it. The title is deliberately provocative. As Abadir has argued in an article for Cartography of Darkness, electronic music has spent decades equating novelty with the future, often reproducing the same cyberpunk imagery, dystopian fantasies and technological narratives inherited from the 1980s and 1990s. For him, that obsession has become a form of nostalgia masquerading as progress, one increasingly detached from the realities of communities living through war, authoritarianism and displacement. The Primitivist proposes another direction altogether: creativity rooted not in speculative futures but in sustained engagement with living musical heritage and the political urgency of the present. That shift is immediately audible. If Mutate revolved around the Egyptian maqsoum rhythm, this EP opens its vocabulary to rhythmic traditions and performance practices from across the Arab world. The opening “Habban” takes its name from the Gulf bagpipe, a celebratory folk instrument associated with communal dancing and percussion ensembles. Rather than sampling tradition as an exotic signifier, Abadir absorbs its rhythmic logic into a contemporary club framework where darbuka, khishba, mijwiz and intricate hand-clapping patterns become structural rather than decorative elements. The ecstatic propulsion of “The Primitivist” and the playful destabilisation of “Pass & Go” continue that trajectory, while the closing “This Is Not Another Maqsoum” knowingly acknowledges — and moves beyond — the rhythmic strategy that defined his previous album. What remains constant throughout Abadir’s catalogue is his concern with transformation. Each record asks a different question, yet all are linked by the same compositional impulse: taking existing sonic materials — speech, liturgy, social media, club music or regional traditions — and discovering how they can be reimagined without losing their historical or cultural specificity. The result is music that consistently resists easy categorisation. It is uncompromisingly contemporary, yet never relies on futurist rhetoric to justify its newness. In an electronic music landscape still eager to describe unfamiliar sounds as “futuristic,” The Primitivist offers a persuasive alternative. It suggests that innovation need not emerge from imagined worlds or technological fantasies. Sometimes it begins by listening more closely to the present and to histories that have always been there, waiting to be heard. photo by Omar Elkafrawy To helps us see beyond the future, we reached out directly to Abadir. The Primitivist presents itself as a rejection of electronic music’s long-standing fascination with futurism. You’ve argued that futurist narratives often reflect Eurocentric ideas of progress while overlooking the lived realities of communities experiencing war or authoritarianism. Once you reject futurism as the dominant framework, what new possibilities does “primitivism” open up for composition? Does it change the way you think about rhythm, sound design or even the social function of club music? My rejection of anything related to futurism has been going for five years, and each year it becomes more radical. I think this makes sense to me at the moment, since the future, futurism and the futuristic have been the main focus in electronic music since the 80’s (if not even before that) to identify what’s new, what’s next and the unheard for the western ears. This narrative of futurism has been already ruling for 40 years, which makes it outdated for me and repetitive to the maximum, to the point where it’s now reduced to a marketing label. It became a habit to link newness to the future, and unfortunately there has been a lack of critique to this idea, or attempts to link creativity and newness to something else other than futurism. It’s even nostalgic that futurism in electronic music is still somehow based on the same concepts, sounds and perspectives that once existed in the 80’s or the 90’s. There have been cycles of criticizing Mark Fisher’s theories, with a general claim that the future didn’t stop and “gotcha Fisher you are wrong”, because X or Y (from the global north) made “futuristic” music. Honestly, this argument is haunted by an outdated vision of what futuristic music means, it’s also haunted by the urge of futurism. That’s nostalgia for futurism (which is different from Fisher’s concept of lost futures) that used to exist decades ago. It’s paradoxical, and in that sense futurism is eating itself. But I think this sort of discussion doesn’t fit the Arabic context because we have different realities and priorities. With the exception of Afrofuturism, the futuristic narrative is escapist and out of touch with the present. It chooses progress and speed rather than understanding and facing the present. The narrative for years has been about fetishising dystopia or the other opposite, techno-optimism led by the “punchline” of “Let’s imagine a future where…” I see both narratives out of touch with reality, especially now. Being able to think like that is a kind of luxury, rather than living the hard present reality which is unfolding in front of our eyes on a daily basis. So at least, an action must be taken to change that, and actions happen in the present. Once we reach a point where present issues are kind of fixed, then we can have the time and luxury to speculate, think about the future and imagine it. More thoughts about this topic can be found in this essay I wrote last year. I chose the term Primitivism as a provocation, a way to say I’m happy I’m not futuristic, I’m busy with the present and I’m inspired by a deeply rooted music heritage. This way of thinking is definitely inspiring because making this claim means that I need to listen, revisit, read and learn a lot about music from the Arab region on the technical, cultural and historical level. During the last few years I learned a lot about Maqamat, rhythms from different parts of the Arab region. As you said, this also had an impact on sound design, because you can easily tell that the sound design in The Primitivist and my coming project is different from what’s in Kitbashing and Ison. On Mutate, the maqsoum rhythm acted almost as the album’s organising principle, whereas The Primitivist draws from a much broader range of rhythmic traditions and instrumental references from Iraq, Kuwait, Syria and Palestine. Tracks such as “Habban”, “The Primitivist” and “This Is Not Another Maqsoum” feel less concerned with hybridising genres than with rethinking the vocabulary of club music itself. How did your compositional approach change between these two records, and did moving beyond maqsoum also change the way you thought about rhythm? Usually I tend to link my projects together, as well as old and fresh ideas. What starts as a sound or an idea in one project will be revisited and developed more a few years later. You can trace that between Pause/Stutter/Uh/Repeat and Kitbashing or Ison, and between Mutate and The Primitivist. This marks the continuity of my work. Maqsoum was the center of Mutate, next to the influence of other club genres that I listen to and DJ. I wasn’t making club music before Mutate, so it made sense to me to start with a sound I’m familiar with and stuck in my memory, which is Maqsoum. It was fun mixing Jungle and Footwork or Jersey with sped up and cut up Maqsoum samples, to come up with a mutated club sound. In The Primitivist I decided to focus more on Arabic rhythms and dropping the influences of other club genres. During a 3 year period I got attracted to sounds from the countries you mentioned and I extended my knowledge to further other rhythmic patterns. The result was working with rhythmic sounds related to Dahhiya, Dabke, simulating a real drummer playing the Khishba or using the Sharbaka, which is a hand clapping technique rooted in the Arabian Gulf, especially in Kuwait. In my coming project, I’m going deeper in sound design, and more complex patterns with a focus on variations in time signatures. There is a striking tension throughout the EP between recognisable Arab instruments—mijwiz pipes, darbuka, khishba, brass timbres—and an approach to rhythm and sound design that remains uncompromisingly contemporary. As someone who has also been exploring Arabic maqamat and instrumental playing techniques in your more recent work, how do you avoid turning these traditions into cultural signifiers or markers of authenticity, allowing them instead to remain living musical materials? I think the idea is about avoiding orientalist and self-orientalist cliches, or lazy fusion, in addition to finding this common ground between the familiar and the unfamiliar, with surprise elements. Once you hear a Mijwiz or a brass synth for instance, you will get that sense of “yes I know that”, then twisting the expectations is the next crucial step. If I hear a Rast or Huzam or Bayati maqam used by an Arabic producer, I will see it as normal. But creativity appears depending on some other factors such as: the articulation and ornamentation in maqamat, the modulation between maqamat, how the producer is implementing these maqamat with drum patterns, how the sound design is made, how the arrangement is done and the structure is built. Here you have a lot of options to twist the expectations. Yet, I still admire the musicians who are maintaining old traditions as they are, because we need that now in our region more than any time before, given the external threat by the infamous pariah state, liberal capitalist “values”, A.I, the Dubaification of our region. This is the very material reality we face and we have to deal with in the present, so again, what future exactly are we talking about? Koleyet El Banat – photo by Omar Elkafrawy Your work sits at an unusual intersection of artistic practice and critical writing. As the editor of the electronic music section at Ma3azef, you’re constantly analysing how electronic music is written about, categorised and historicised. Has writing criticism changed the way you make music? Conversely, has producing records like The Primitivist made you more critical of the vocabulary and frameworks through which electronic music — particularly music from the Arab world — is discussed in western publications? My criticism towards the vocabulary and frameworks used in western publications as well as the westernised Arabic ones has always been there. I also believe that the music journalist or the critic has to read, follow and listen a lot, a good level of curiosity is required. I’m trying to do my best with that, so my critique can have some basis. Maybe The Primitivist is a result of that. It’s about how to express critique through a medium other than writing; proposing that we don’t need to be obsessed with the future or futurism to be creative, alternatively, we can be focused in the present or we can draw inspiration from our cultural roots. The present is here already. The same applies on Kitbashing by the way, one can theorise about its concept in an essay or a book, but I wanted to represent the concept sonically. Definitely, working in criticism has made me think differently about my own music, because it has made me much more self-critical. My music projects are slow cooked, and each one starts with a simple question: why am I doing this or what am I trying to say? This question can be frustrating or provocative to some artists, but for me it makes total sense and it’s the main critical question behind every project.ِ During the process, I can be very critical and harsh towards myself, but it helps me a lot. With Kitbashing, you proposed feeding on the algorithm rather than feeding it, transforming the sounds of social media into compositional material. In retrospect, do you think the algorithm can ever truly be subverted, or does every attempt at resisting it inevitably become another form of participation? On an individual level, we can benefit from the algorithm, whether by using it for learning purposes, an introduction to something, being informed about cultural or political topics, or simply watching something fun, because we need a break. Apart from that, ِI wish in general that the algorithm is subverted for something good and I think this has to be collectively done. Take for instance the non-commercial electronic music scene which is now driven by the algorithmic scrolling mentality, everyone from the curators, to the spaces, to the artists, to the press, to the crowd, is so invested in an app. Everything has been highly dependent on Instagram. It has become the main way to be heard and seen and that’s exhausting and frustrating. A couple of slides or a polished one minute video from the peak of a live or DJ set defines an artist. But imagine that the press and curators are relatively withdrawing from Instagram, this can have a good impact on producers and DJs, they will spend less time on the app, and post less, only when it’s necessary. This will make the crowd spend more time listening and reading, and artists will only focus on their music and their work. That would be ideal, isn’t it? (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: What happens if the sun disappears? The question lingered over the stage at Viljandi Folk Festival on the morning its closing day. Tell Your Birds brought it there, playing songs from a still unreleased record in front of a crowd for the first time. Kristīne Tukre‘s concert kokle carried the melodies, Vija Moore‘s balafon sat under them, Kärt Tambet‘s bowed hiiu kannel cut across both, and everything the three of them played ran through Simone Spampinato‘s processing. They sang in Estonian and Latvian at once, each keeping the language they grew up speaking. Some of the material comes from those same traditions, chopped up and rebuilt inside the band’s own songs. The rest belongs to no repertoire at all, written on the chance that one day it might. Straight after the set, in the last hour before Tell Your Birds broke apart for the rest of the summer, we sat down with the four of them not far from the stage, with a temperamental recorder giving us a hard time and cutting out every few minutes. Our chat eventually fell into the band’s own working rhythm: a burst, a stop, a burst. Tukre and Spampinato live in Helsinki, Tambet in Viljandi, Moore in Riga. They get a few days together, write everything in that stretch, then go back to their own cities until the next one. In the hour before they scattered, they talked about where a tradition comes from and what you have to know before using it, about melodies written for a time that has not happened yet, and about the syllables that decide which language a song ends up in. Tell Your Birds started with a student project. All four met at the Sibelius Academy in Helsinki, in different departments, and Tambet dates the band from there: “We came together as a band back in 2023, but back then it was a very specific project. It was Vija [Moore], who is our percussionist, her bachelor concert project in Sibelius Academy in Finland, where we all studied together.” The concert called for soundscape music written for one place and recorded in it, and the place Moore picked was a forest near Ērgļi, a village in Latvia. They hauled the balafon, the percussion, the violin and the kokle out among the trees and played there, birds and insects carrying on around them and ending up on the tape along with everything else. For Spampinato that set the method for everything after it: “it was the first project where we all get together and thought, we recorded everything outside. We tried to record the instruments as they were part of the soundscape in that sense.” That turned into Pause in Nature, then Carry on with Hope, out on 1 November 2024. One year later they wanted more room to move, and Tambet marks autumn 2025 as the turn: “to write together and to think of music more widely, maybe not so specifically as we had done before“. Moore had been waiting for it: “I like that with this new music, we got to put it all together.” There was a lot to put together. The four met inside one institution and arrived there from four directions, and Moore starts with the two furthest from folk: “Simone comes from sound art, electronics, different sound design type of experience and worldview. And then Kristīne comes from a contemporary composition and contemporary kantele playing. Also, Kristīne is interested in baroque music.” She and Tambet are the two who came up in folk, she through percussion, Tambet through singing and the violin. The spread is the point for Moore: “Each of us have a different genre outlook. I think it all comes together in our music, and it’s very interesting.“ Tukre’s own route ran through the classical kantele, though her instrument at home is the kokle. The Estonian kannel, the Latvian kokle and the Finnish kantele are cousins in one family of box zithers, and the family resemblance is where it gets interesting for her: “We have a very interesting phenomenon here in the Baltics and in Finland. We have these string instruments; they’re similar, but at the same time very different. They have different names, but we, musicians, try to come together.” The players of all three look across the borders to each other’s instruments. She did exactly that, a kokle player going to Helsinki to learn the kantele at the Sibelius Academy: “That’s how I got to Finland. I got to meet Viia, Gert and Simone, and we started the band.“ Coming together now happens across three countries, which turns rehearsals and recording sessions into an exercise of dates, plans and travel tickets, so they work in blocks: several days in one of the three places, everything at once, then dispersal. For Moore the two halves stay separate: “We just intensively get into the music for those couple of days, and then go back to our real lives.” Where those blocks happen feeds the music too. “I also think us meeting for intensive times in different places has played a big role in the music. Because when we have come to Viljandi, we get to see into the Viljandi life, and we get to see into the whole Estonian culture, even social culture. It plays such a big role of explaining what a tradition means. And then also going to Latvia all together, that was the missing puzzle pieces.” Estonia, Latvia and Finland have all had their turn. Italy is still waiting, as Spampinato points out: “We have not been to Italy. What a terrible thing!” The residencies have gone further than rehearsal rooms and taken the four into each other’s family homes, which Moore counts as its own kind of source material: “In our residencies, it’s very nice that we’ve met each other’s families because families represent culture in a whole other coded way, it’s something not explainable by words.” What comes back from those weeks is a songbook the band builds itself. Tambet traces the bulk of it to the four of them: “Most of the music is actually original music that we have composed together, or separately, but brought it to this group.” Folk melodies feed into it, and so do myths, texts and lyrics that arrive as words alone. Before using any of it, Tambet wants the origin and the original purpose clear: “there’s a lot of using a tradition in music. You have to be aware of it, and translating it to others. It’s highly important that we’re aware where it’s coming from and what the original intention behind that tradition is, so we can translate it into our own musical language.” The traditions Spampinato grew up with are not the ones on the table. He comes from Sicily, but his folk roots lie in Ciociaria, a historical region of southern Lazio: “My folk background is actually from Ciociaria, not Sicilian.” What he brings instead comes from sound art, electronics and sound design, where the tradition is the sound itself: “My background is more about sound. What do we do with every little sound?” Put that question to folk music and you get the music he admires most: “I’m really a huge fan of experimental French folk music, Sourdure for example, and I think we are trying to get into that.” In practice it means cutting material up and putting it back together: “What we use a lot is chopping and sampling, this kind of collage, things colliding. Sometimes they’re all together, sometimes we really like the contrast.” The same goes for how the four handle it on stage, where the play is in the treatment, not the tunes: “Maybe the songs don’t seem that playful, but how we manage our material is super playful. Viia is playing with four mallets [on the balafon], I’m on the synth and then the guitar. It’s collage in that sense.“ The same collage habit carries into the lyrics, starting with language. Sometimes the four sing three languages at the same time, like a group chanting together, each in their own language instead of settling on a shared one. For Tukre, that’s the point: “We don’t make these language compromises.” The words themselves usually start from folk songs and folk tales, which she reworks before they can be sung now: “The language tends to be quite archaic and doesn’t always fit with the world we live in. So we like to shape it a little and add some reference points we can relate to, but keep the original idea our ancestors had in their folk songs.” The shaping mostly falls to her, in Spampinato’s words “the poet of the band“. A song’s meaning is often sketched in English first, but the language it ends up in is chosen by ear, and for Moore sound decides it: “We’re a lot based on the sound, so what sound are we searching for? That’s where the language plays a big role.” Syllable counts settle much of it: “Some songs require Estonian lyrics, you can just feel it fits better, and some songs are Latvian. The number of syllables each language uses for one word can be different, so we use that to our advantage. How many syllables do we need? And just the pure phonetics of it.” Their latest single, “pa saulei”, is written and sung in Latvian and takes the idea down to a single word. Saule is sun, pasaule is world, and pa saulei means following the sun. Moore sums up the trick: “If you add these little syllables before and after it, it can change the meaning.“ “pa saulei”, like everything they put out, never leaves the band’s hands. The four handle the engineering, mixing and visuals themselves, and for Spampinato that’s the most independent way to work: “We do everything by ourselves: recording, mixing, visuals. It’s holistic, even though I don’t like the word. It’s maybe the most independent thing you can do, just do everything.” The setting shifts every time. Their debut was made outdoors in Ērgļi, a village in Latvia, with the instruments caught as part of the surrounding soundscape. The follow-up, due in April 2027, moves indoors to Moore’s house and home studio: “We think we need that kind of closeness, but still the comfort.” The shift is deliberate: “I don’t know what the next album will be, probably in a spaceship. But every time we try to come up not only with new music, but with a new way of approaching it.“ That album, due in April 2027, will carry the material they played at Viljandi Folk, and a single built on a traditional Estonian horn melody comes first, this September. A short tour follows in November, with Helsinki confirmed for 20 November as part of the Global Club Nights series, then release concerts in April in Latvia, Estonia and, they hope, Helsinki again. For anyone hearing them for the first time, the band’s own introduction says it best: “Tell Your Birds is a four-person music collective of musicians from Latvia, Estonia and Italy. We play our original compositions with collages of Estonian, Latvian and Italian traditional folk melodies and archive recordings and texts.“     Tell Your Birds released "pa saulei" in June, with the album due in April 2027 and everything in between turning up on their Instagram       The post Interview: Tell Your Birds – Writing a Tradition for Later (September 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: Tell Your Birds由四位分别来自爱沙尼亚、拉脱维亚、意大利的西贝柳斯音乐学院学生组成，横跨赫尔辛基、维尔扬迪、里加三城，以集中数日创作而后各自离散的协作模式工作。专辑将波罗的海传统乐器——拉脱维亚 kokle、爱沙尼亚 hiiu kannel、西非 balafon——与现场电子处理和野外录音编织在一起，音乐素材既有从本地民歌传统中拆解重组的部分，也有为尚未发生的时代全新谱写的旋律。歌词以爱沙尼亚语和拉脱维亚语同时呈现，每位成员保留各自的母语发音。早期作品源自Vija Moore的学士毕业项目，在拉脱维亚Ērgļli村附近的森林中录制，将乐器声与鸟鸣虫声共同捕捉进磁带，奠定了此后田野录音与器乐融合的方法论基础。新作进一步拓宽创作自由度，从特定场景声音设计转向更开放的共构写作。整体呈现出欧洲北部传统器乐、当代作曲技法与实验电子处理的多重交汇。

items.body: Our third iteration of the " Sculpting Silence " series, brings us to France, for a trio with Alexandra Grimal on saxophones, voice, harmonium, nōkan, shakuhachi, Naoto Yamagishi on percussions and Alexandre Saada on piano and harmonium. The title, Marée Basse , is French for “low tide”: the moment when the sea withdraws, leaving behind a wide, empty stretch of beach scattered with shells, tiny creatures, and fragments the waves have carried ashore. The music evokes much the same landscape. It takes this open space for granted, allowing the notes of saxophone, piano, and percussion to appear sparsely, sometimes only for brief moments before disappearing again. All three musicians are minimalists, deeply attentive to the overall sound yet reluctant to impose themselves upon it, as though the tones themselves should determine whether, and when, they wish to interact. Every sound feels tender and fragile, unobtrusive and gentle—and often completely absent. Silence is not merely the space between the notes; it is an essential part of the music itself. This is particularly striking in the thirty-minute second track, where, roughly halfway through, there is almost a full minute of near silence, with only faint crackling sounds barely audible in the background. When the music gradually returns, the instrumentation has subtly shifted: the harmonium introduces a handful of sustained tones, joined by Grimal's wordless singing, equally elongated and sensitive. Towards the end of the piece, the sound becomes fuller and more agitated, as though a sudden gust of wind were stirring the waves and awakening the distant cries of seagulls. Once again, silence plays an essential role in this music, much as it does in Japanese art, which has fascinated Grimaldi in recent years. Here, absence is not a lack but a presence of its own—a space in which the smallest sounds can emerge, linger for a moment, and then quietly disappear. Enjoy! Listen and download from Bandcamp . items.body: Cuban drummer Francisco Mela’s free jazz odyssey continues on four new releases, writes Daniel Spicer in The Wire 512 Francisco Mela Carnaval De Oriente 577 CD/DL Jowee Omicil & Francisco Mela OM BasH! Village DL Rafael Zaldivar Zaldivar/McBride/Mela: Meeting In New York Vol 1 577 DL Matthew Putman/Hill Greene/Francisco Mela Bright Sun Outside 577 CD/DL Cuban drummer Francisco Mela’s route into the mysteries of free jazz has been a circuitous one. He started out as a teenager working in the bands of Latin jazz pianists and fellow countrymen Emiliano Salvador and Gabriel Hernandez before moving to the US at the turn of the millennium and building a reputation as an in-demand straightahead jazz drummer, playing with Joe Lovano and enjoying nearly a decade in pianist McCoy Tyner’s trio. Following Tyner’s death in 2020 and the forced hiatus of the pandemic, Mela emerged with a new fascination for and commitment to freedom, forging a fruitful partnership with the Brooklyn based 577 label and collaborating with heavy-hitters including William Parker, Cooper-Moore and Matthew Shipp. His journey is not entirely without precedent. Milford Graves cut his teeth in the early 1960s playing congas and timbales in Latin and Afro-Cuban outfits and led The Milford Graves Latino Quartet, featuring a young pianist by the name of Chick Corea, before a 1962 encounter with the volcanic eruptions of Elvin Jones alongside Tyner in John Coltrane’s quartet inspired him to turn to the drum kit and become a key architect of the mid-60s free jazz New Thing, entirely rewiring the possibilities of time and timbre in the process. In Cuban pianist Rafael Zaldivar’s trio, Mela teams up with Christian McBride, who held bass duties in Corea’s trio with drummer Brian Blade, as heard on the 2013 live album Trilogy. In fact, on Meeting In New York Vol 1, Zaldivar at times channels a strikingly similar feel to Corea’s sophisticated and sentimental tunefulness, embraced by McBride’s muscular lyricism. It’s a temptation Mela resolutely resists, avoiding Blade’s deep swing in favour of a constant flickering fizz of cymbals and snare, dancing playfully around the idea of time. At other moments, Zaldivar summons puckish declamations more akin to Paul Bley, eliciting a brawnier churn from Mela punctuated by sudden gunshot snare cracks while, in a diaphanous free ballad, his subtle brush work shushes and sighs in gaseous textures. Here, McBride – not often heard in a free context – sounds a little out of place, cramming as many notes as possible into solos perhaps more suited to a contemporary post-bop milieu. There’s no such mismatch in the trio with pianist Matthew Putman, where the low end is held down by Hilliard Greene, a bassist with considerable avant garde credentials, having worked with the likes of pianists Don Pullen and Cecil Taylor, and saxophonist Charles Gayle. Bright Sun Outside navigates more familiar free jazz terrain and isn’t afraid to ramble. Even some of its fairly brief improvisations, lasting just a few minutes, convey a sense of loose and leisurely meandering, with Putman flicking out spontaneous melodic gambits that seem quite content to never fully commit to a destination – like a succession of half-formed thoughts bubbling up in an unhurried internal monologue. Mela is happily along for the ride, laying out a rattling commentary dominated by an arrestingly dry snare, each stroke deftly placed with neat precision. When Greene leans into rasping arco shrieks and Putman chops out sudden staccato stabs, Mela flexes his muscles with a more aggressive energy, like fresh flames springing up from glowing embers. Mela’s first solo album Carnaval De Oriente proposes a wholly different mood. Inspired by the sounds of the eponymous street carnival heard in his childhood, he rolls around the drum kit – revealing a loose, earthy sound reminiscent of Graves – adding shakers, cowbell and sundry percussion. All the while, he chirps spontaneous vocal chants and snatches of song that recall percussionist/vocalist Juno Lewis’s mythically resonant Afro-Creole vocals on his song “Kulu Sé Mama (Juno Sé Mama)”, recorded with John Coltrane in 1965. On one track, Mela tinkers with rudimentary innocence on a glockenspiel; on another, he picks clumsily at an acoustic guitar. What he lacks in chops, he makes up for with unabashed enthusiasm. Whistling absentmindedly and chatting contentedly to himself, he sounds like he’s having a fine time. When the full kit breaks through in a burst of dense polyrhythms, you can pretty much hear the smile on his face. His concise improvised duets with Canadian-Haitian multi-instrumentalist Jowee Omicil are in a similar vein, as the pair explore the shared musical traditions of Haiti and Cuba. On saxophones and clarinet, Omicil displays some of the loquacious unpredictability of Eric Dolphy, while Mela rolls out a nimble undertow that occasionally comes close to a standard jazz sound, replete with full-bodied rolls and tumbles. Omicil’s lip-smacking pocket trumpet works Mela up into a frenzied freakout of ecstatic vocal cries. Intuitive piano splashes invite a thoughtful drizzle of snare and ride. Mela sings with lusty abandon and thwacks out hambone rhythms on his own body. Again, a palpable sense of spontaneous joy reigns throughout. There’s an obvious similarity to Don Cherry’s duets with drummer Ed Blackwell, as documented on the twin Mu albums: while reaching back past the dim origins of jazz, Mela and Omicil conduct imaginary Pangaean rituals bursting with the same omnivorous exuberance that colours all of Mela’s music. This review appears in The Wire 512 along with many other reviews of new and recent records, books, films, festivals and more. To read them all, pick up a copy of the magazine in our online shop. Wire subscribers can also read the issue in our online magazine library.
items._cn_summary: 古巴鼓手弗朗西斯科·梅拉在多张新专辑中延续其自由爵士探索之旅。评论追溯了他从拉丁爵士乐队走向McCoy Tyner三重奏、再到与577厂牌合作转向自由即兴的音乐路径，将其与Milford Graves早年经历相类比。重点剖析的四张专辑展现了他对时间和音色的持续解构：在与Zaldivar的三重奏中，他以闪烁的镲片和小鼓编织拒绝深潜式的自由律动，回应钢琴家时而接近Paul Bley的诙谐宣叙；与Putman和Greene的合作则因贝斯手的深厚先锋背景而更为契合。评论细致分析了梅拉在不同编制下的鼓棒选择与肌理变化，凸显其作为当代自由爵士鼓手的独特声音身份与跨文化语境下的创作脉络。

items.body: This ensemble will always carry a deeply personal connotation for me. In 2015, they released their first album, Rune , at a time when I was hospitalised for two weeks, waking at irregular hours. Despite the dire circumstances, listening to Earth Tongues at four in the morning, alone in the darkness, was a strange and deeply soothing experience. There was something about the ensemble’s careful, almost cautious little sounds—the tiny sonic points that gradually accumulated into a landscape that absorbed, captivated, and ultimately elevated you—that created a uniquely powerful listening experience. It is difficult to explain how important it became for me to return to this music again and again, and how much it taught me about the value of life, the value of art, and the value of improvised music. When everything collapses around you—and inside you—you begin to realise that whatever remains, however small or fragmented, can still be enough to create something meaningful. You learn to cherish the smallest isolated event - " at least I still have this ", to pay attention to what might otherwise go unnoticed, and to welcome the spontaneous connections with and between people who can, together, create beauty out of those tiny fragments of luck. And in many ways, that is what this music does. Little sounds, little fragments, little pieces surrounded by silence, which, when brought together, can still constitute something beautiful, something meaningful, something valuable. It gave me hope against all odds, and with it a profound insight: to cherish every moment. Life is not necessarily a long story with a clear plot. Perhaps it is instead a collection of small, random events—fragments that, taken together, become a life, and that are all worth living. The trio, so many years later are still Joe Moffett on trumpet, Dan Peck on tuba, and Carlo Costa on percussion. Like their previous albums, their sound is deeply organic, drawing on the textures and rhythms of the natural world: the drip of water, pebbles falling, animals growling, birds twittering. Each of the three long tracks has its own distinct character, while the music gradually evolves from pointillist blips into increasingly stretched-out tones in the final piece. Very slowly, almost imperceptibly, these scattered sonic fragments begin to coalesce. The subtlety of this shift is deliberate, shaped by carefully considered compositional ideas and structures. Silence is an essential part of their music—the white space between colours, an open realm of possibility waiting to be filled. What makes their work so compelling is the extraordinary value they give to each individual sound, with an intense attention to precision, texture, and timbral quality. When you enter their music attentively, it seems to slow down rational thought itself, allowing you to surrender to the sound and, for a while, simply be the music. items._cn_summary: Earth Tongues 乐团由小号、长号与打击乐组成，以极简的点状声响构建音乐景观。专辑延续其自然主义美学，将水滴、砾石、动物低鸣等声音素材融入即兴演奏，强调每个音符的精确度与质感。三首长篇曲目各自具备独特性格，声响从最初碎片化的微弱脉冲，在末曲中逐渐延展为绵长的持续音，几乎不可察觉地汇聚成完整的织体。沉默被视作构图的留白，与音响本身拥有同等地位。乐队赋予每一个孤立声响以崇高价值，要求聆听者放慢理性思维，全然沉浸于声音之中，从中体验生命与艺术在碎片中重构意义的可能。

items.body: Actress Radical Frame Making his return to the Ninja Tune label, Darren Cunningham practices typical elusiveness with doleful piano stabs amidst pounding surf and ambient textures Radical Frame by Actress Try to recall an Actress track and you won’t bring a melody or rhythm back. You’ll find only a noir sensation, the faint memory of wading through a city’s hazy silence at four in the morning, alone, but with something in the air around you that the skin registers before the mind does. A rusting Weltschmerz bleeds through Darren Cunningham’s music, dissolving evanescent motifs into lasting affect. Over twenty years into his career, Radical Frame sees the UK producer continue to explore music that resists forgetting. The almost preternatural allure of Cunningham’s first proper solo... The post Actress – Radical Frame appeared first on The Quietus.
items._cn_summary: 这是英国制作人Darren Cunningham（艺名Actress）回归Ninja Tune厂牌的作品，延续了他二十余年职业生涯中一以贯之的创作路径。整张专辑回避了清晰的旋律与节奏记忆，转而营造一种阴郁的都市夜行质感——凌晨四点独自穿行于雾霭笼罩的城市，空气中弥漫着某种皮肤先于意识感知到的东西。钢琴短促的刺点穿行于汹涌的声浪与环境质感之间，瞬息的动机消融为持久的情绪印记。评论指出，Cunningham的音乐带有一种近乎超自然的吸引力，模糊了氛围、节拍与实验声响的边界，属于典型的Ninja Tune体系下偏向地下与前卫的电子探索。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Recorded in London at Orange Recording Studios LTD. December 9-12, 1970 and then released early in 1971 by Global Records.A1. "Thursday Morning Sunrise" (11:38) not the opening I was expecting--ever--from a 1971 prog album much less a Jazz-Rock Fusion one. The deep, low, heavily distorted organ play sounds like Markus Pajakkala's baritone saxes and bass clarinet on his (memorable) 2017 Brutopianisti album! When other instruments finally join in they're all grotesquely distorted: Eberhard's wild (and virtuosic) electric bass, Siggi Schwab's Sonny-Sharrock/Arto Lindsay-like electric guitar, even the drumming/percussion work of Fred Braceful and Roland Wittich is wild. I wouldn't call this "Free Jazz" like something from Ornette Coleman, John Coltrane's post-A Love Supreme period, or Sun Ra's Arkestra, but a fusion of these with experimental sound explorations and, in the second half, the incorporation of sophisticated African rhythms with even some from the more avant-garde realms of Classical Music. I am blown away, incredibly impressed, and find myself incredibly entertained as well as fully enjoying this trail-blazing exercise in boundary-obliteration. Could this album have been a key food source for the inspiration of soon-to-appear bands like UNIVERS ZERO or AREA?--certainly this type of music (19.25/20)A2. "Lady Blue" (3:03) now, hearing this amazing song that combines Beatnik poetry-delivery musical formats with Classical Music choral traditions, I find myself asking whether or not Wolfgang, Eberhard, Siggi, and/or Fred were fans or progeny of George Russell's School of Esoteric Musics while George was a professor in residence at Sweden's Lund University. I absolutely love this! Another totally unexpected song that I find myself returning to over and over to try to fathom its creative scope. (9.75/10)A3. "Mellodroma 2a" (5:10) more choir appearances open this--from a distance--before Siggi's acoustic guitar enters playing with congas and double bass in what can only be descrived as a Folk Rock tune akin to something by Bert and John, The Pentangle, or The Incredible String Band. And the choir continues to make small appearances! These guys are amazing! The diverse interests and forms for their musical expression seems to have no bounds! Lite drums join in but it's the hand percussion that dominates with Eberhard's double bass Wonderful! Another song that totally took me by surprise and which lures me back again and again for repeated listens as I try desperately to fathom their thinking and desires. In the fourth minute there is a lull in which Siggi gets to show off a little more of his acoustic guitar skills, but then the rest of the band re-joins for a rousing finish with percussion and organ really bringing it (though no return of the choir). Wonderful! (9.333/10)B1. "Raga" (16:17) apparently Siggi Schwab had really gotten into a huge variety of World Music stringed instruments--and especially stringed instruments prevalent in India--like the but also zithers, psaltries, This track was actually written by Siggi, who is credited with a vast array of traditional, ethnic, and Indian stringed instruments on the record. Among the highly zither-like instruments he plays on the album and track are the swarmandal (credited as "surmandel") and the bulbul tarang. Siggi also contributed sitar, veena, tambura, and sarangi to the album's rich, psychedelic raga-rock sound. Eberhard, Fred, Roland, and Wolfgang do their best to provide inputs that they think will enhance, embellish, and not detract from Siggi's reverence for his Indian studies. I find the use of the full drum kit in the seventh through ninth minute to be a bit overwhelming and domineering to the Indian spirit being expressed but, it's a good awareness experiment and, fortunately, it ends so that the song can move into a new, more-percussion-centric passage--one that contains Eberhard's talking drum like bass play as well as a lot of intertwined and improvisationally-reactive percussion threads, gradually embellished by trumpet and, later, cymbal-crashing drum kit and distorted synth string sounds. Things quite down again in the sixteenth minute, leaving Siggi and his mates to finish the song with a thin palette of almost-incidental noises and percussives to usher Siggi's surmandel out. (By the way, Fred's drum play over this last sections is much more tasteful and respectful--much less invasive and brutal.) Another surreally-unexpected and eminently-enjoyable song that makes me wish I had been there--wish I could have been present for these practice and recording sessions as well as known these remarkably intrepid musicians! (28.25/30) B2. "Milkstreets" (4:15) a relatively unstructured melange of natural and unnatural (treated and electonic) sounds, many coming from African and Indian traditions. Interesting and historically significant (like the work of John Cage, Terry Riley, Herbie Hancock, Area and so many other adventurists). (8.875/10) Total time: 40:23YouTube provided me with three extra/bonus songs that apparently came from the same December 1970 London recording sessions but only saw the light of day (and a public awareness) on a 2008 CD release from the Long Hair label. They are also quite interesting and experimental, allowing for even more display of all the weird instruments that Siggi and Wolfgang had been playing around with. A/five stars; an absolute masterpiece of experimental and leading-edge Jazz-Rock Fusion. HIGHLY recommended and ESSENTIAL for any J-R Fusion and Progressive Rock fan.

items.body: Happy golden anniversary to the International Computer Music Conference! This special album honors founder David Wessel (1942–2014). The full title of the 2025 theme: Curiosity, Play, Innovation—A 50th Anniversary Celebration of Creativity in Music, Science and Technology. This generous collection showcases electro-acoustic music from around the world. Each piece is intricate and unique, while many touch upon contemporary themes, starting with Jiajing Zhao‘s “Glitchopolis,” a commentary on information overload. The very first sound is that of an alarm, doubled and then tripled, set against London traffic, which begins to fracture, stutter and glitch. Garbled human voices emerge from a processed vat; construction and technology intertwine. A bee – real and metaphoric – buzzes by, followed by a flock of birds, fireworks and a police siren. How many inputs can one brain handle? “Pardon me, ‘scuse me, sorry,” a commuter apologizes at the end. By refusing to mute the signals, the composer imitates the feeling of being overwhelmed, not only aural, but emotionally. “Rumors, approximated” by Shane Turner with Simone Pitot (Delorca) uses algorithms to translate sound into data. The textures are the key, but as patterns emerge, questions of value arise: are these patterns authentic or unintentional? And how much of the human remains after technology has had its say? While Pitot purposely subjected her vocals to this process, other parts of life are unwittingly fed to the whims of the machine. Zeo Lin‘s Escape, whose opening minutes flirt with the dance floor, is filled with glass crashes and computer beeps, percussion and synth, piano and breath, representing a clash between the organic and the electronic, its movements marked by the click of a cassette. At the end a church bell tolls, only to by subsumed by static. Daniele Valenti‘s “CAN you hear them?” is particularly clever, derived almost entirely from the timbres of cans. Without knowing this, one might only guess at the nature of these sounds. The knowledge allows one to lean in,, to cherish the sounds made by the humble object that one often kicks down the road or discards without any attention to its aural qualities. Can a can sound like traffic, or rain? Yes, it CAN. In contrast, “Hammerklavier” uses the piano as its acoustic source, with Antonio Argentieri doing pretty much everything but playing the keys. Think of Matmos’ Ultimate Care II, which performed a similar feat with a washing machine. Few would ever guess that this is a piano piece, which exponentially increases its appeal. How does it feel to be “an international student with limited English proficiency” in London? Hongquan Yang and Fan Zu attempt to translate the experience in “Rambling,” starting with a traditional classroom speech about sound, then feeding it through echo, loop and reverb, injecting their own language to return the favor. Soon everyone is confused, yet finds common ground in the tempo and the playful approach. Passing grade! The chimes and choral tones of the beautifully titled “A Poem for Little Things” turn out to have been taken from children’s toys; as the mother of twins, Chung Eun Kim‘s aural environment has been altered, and she has responded by altering it right back, finding rhythm and melody, wonder and awe, in a castanet, maraca or toy xylophone. “Decorate beauty” is the concept behind Peter Dickson Lopez and Ensemble MISE-EN. “Mise En Series I” begins as a pure chamber piece before the electro-acoustic elements enter; the timbre approaches drone, as the instruments swell with sound, underpinned by pensive electronics. As if coming full cycle, Liu Yurai‘s “The Shackle” is inspired by a visit to the thousand-year-old Daci Temple, an oasis of peace located in the heart of Chengdu. The contrast between peace and overload (as first addressed in “Glitchopolis”) is palpable. Tapping and texting sounds overlap and threaten to undo all calm; a train clacks by; passengers chatter. Soon the bicycle bells are replaced by temple bells, the incoherent conversations with chants, the traffic with birdsong, and a sense of balance is restored. Unfortunately, albeit realistically, the outside world keeps rushing back in. “Seascape Serenity” readjusts the scene. Yu Chia Kuo and SinYu Deng pack the soundscape with hydrophone recordings that reflect the ecosystems of Taiwan. Just as one wished for the serenity of the temple in “The Shackle,” one wishes for humans to stop polluting the biophony of this piece. And yet, this is part of the lesson: that marine life is at least as stressed as we are and that we have caused both. While the piece attempts a happy ending, increasing the number of species calls, one wonders how realistic this might be; the title becomes less a reflection of the piece than an elegy. Taken as a whole, Best of the Listening Rooms demonstrates incredible range while managing to flow beautifully as a whole. The collection is sociologically enlightening yet retains a sense of fun, honoring the theme. Most couples are winding down by their golden anniversary, but we have a feeling that the International Computer Music Conference is just getting started. (Richard Allen)

items._cn_summary: 此专辑为国际计算机音乐会议五十周年纪念合集，致敬创始人David Wessel，收录来自全球的电声音乐作品。每首作品均围绕特定概念展开声音实验：赵佳婧的《Glitchopolis》以警报声与城市交通为素材，通过故障化处理模拟信息过载的感受；Turner与Pitot合作的《Rumors, approximated》用算法将声音转化为数据纹理，探讨机器处理后人类痕迹的留存问题；Zeo Lin的《Escape》以玻璃碎裂、计算机提示音与磁带咔嗒声构建有机与电子的冲突；Valenti的《CAN you hear them?》几乎完全以罐头为声源，揭示日常物体的隐藏音色；Argentieri的《Hammerklavier》以钢琴的非传统演奏方式制造出人意料的声学效果；杨洪全与Zu的《Rambling》则试图以回声、循环与混响翻译国际学生在语言隔阂中的体验。整体专辑展示了当代电声音乐在算法作曲、物件声音化与文化叙事等方面的广阔探索。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 这是一张由内罗毕新厂牌 Cool Waters 发行的跨文化合作专辑，德国裔肯尼亚打击乐手 Sven Kacirek 与本土音乐人 Olith Ratengo 组成的双人组 Odd Okoddo 自 2018 年开始合作，本作特别邀请了 83 岁的肯尼亚东部传统 dodo 唱法歌手 Ogoya Nengo 共同录制。Kacirek 以 Buchla 合成器、手鼓及偶尔的架子鼓构建律动层，电子音色始终作为人声的支撑而非主导，使得 Nengo 与 Ratengo 之间的传统对唱得以凸显。专辑以 'Bara' 为例，合成器多层次复节奏逐渐浮现，最终与两条人声线融为一体；'Sarah' 节奏尖锐，Ratengo 主唱下电子失真在高潮处突现，强化紧迫感。评论指出，'folktronica' 这一标签并不足以概括这类作品的真正价值——它展现了一种跨文化对话的方式，传统根源被推向先锋前沿，革新元素却似已存在千年。

items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.
items.label: Songs of Compassion
items._cn_summary: 这是Dorothy Moskowitz联合前卫作曲家Paladino与诗人Ferrari的合作专辑《Songs of Compassion》，共十一首作品。音乐以钢琴为核心乐器，配合弦乐、木管、合成器泛音与金属质感音效，刻意打破西方和声运动的惯性逻辑，采用非线性的调式结构，让人联想到Steve Reich与Philip Glass的极简重复传统。Moskowitz的演唱如方法派演员般诠释歌词，旋律随意识流起伏，不依附于常规音阶进行，而是让每个词语独立获得重量。歌词兼具政治批判与哲思冥想：从极权主义的同谋机制，到直接引用新纳粹口号的反讽书写，再到对死亡与宇宙位置的沉思。整张专辑延续六十年代抗议歌曲传统，同时以当代视角回应当下分裂的时代氛围，呈现出实验声响与诗性文本的高度统一。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 乐队的第二张专辑延续了首作的风格杂烩路线，成员以废弃物与零碎物件亲手制作各类乐器（如 tassofon、kitchenofon 等），却保持了精准的音准与现代录音品质。专辑跨越多种世界音乐风格：开篇以单簧管演绎克莱兹默曲调并配合人声呼喊；中段融入昆比亚舞曲的西班牙语合唱与拉丁打击乐；同名曲以非洲节拍木鱼、铃铛构建 Afrobeat 氛围；后续曲目则分别呈现桑巴律动与中东迷幻旋律。演奏者在多数曲目中进行即兴发挥，展现出不俗的技巧。整张专辑以杂陈拼贴的方式庆祝人类对节奏与旋律的普遍热爱，同时提醒音乐人总能以最朴素的材料创造声音。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items.body: “The Gray” is the second album by Italian producer Stefano Santi. Four years after his debut album, “JXDY”, the artist draws inspiration from themes such as love, loss, and collapse. He has also enlisted guest vocalists including Meldamor, Castelli, Contre Soirée, and Filmmaker. “The Gray” features a diverse range of influences—sometimes further accentuated by the guest vocalists—yet the album maintains a strong sense of cohesion. The opening track is brilliant, sounding like Shoegaze with subtle Dark-Wave undertones. These two influences remain prominent and, to my ears, constitute the album’s most compelling elements. However, you will also discover touches of Dream-Pop and even a more Dance-oriented track featuring Meldamor. The vocals are produced in a distinctive way, hovering in the background like a mist settling over the songs while still making their mark. Musically, I find the guitar work superb, particularly on the tracks leaning towards Shoegaze. Synth arrangements are also incorporated, at times heightening the atmosphere while adding a fresh dimension to the overall sound. The final track is an instrumental that feels like an outro, but one of exceptional quality. It stands out as a highlight in terms of atmosphere and provides a powerful conclusion to an album filled with gems. “The Gray” is a fantastic record that sounds like a distinctive fusion of several closely related genres. Definitely worth checking out! (Rating:8½). Listen to “Hxlding Time”: Hxlding Time by Never About Never Never is the solo project of Italian producer Stefano Santi, based in Milan. The project debuted with the album “JXDY” on 18 March 2022 (catalog VEYL033) on the Veyl label, recorded as instinct-led material that was not originally planned as a full-length. Santi’s first outside collaboration was a remix of Years Of Denial‘s “City Lights”, a step that carried into his second album, “The Gray”, released via Veyl on 26 June 2026 (catalog VEYL048) and built around guest contributions including Arizona duo Meldamor.

items.body: On the cotton candy sky Written every moment of life For all eternity Wonder why we are even alive Some records come from a scene, some from a city, and some seem to come from that ugly five-minute interval after you have stared at your phone too long and suddenly hate civilization. Faded Flowers, the latest album from Turkish Darkwave duo Ductape, belongs to the third category. It looks around at modern life: crowded rooms, digital selves, obedient routines, private disintegration, and finds a species that has become astonishingly good at maintaining appearances while quietly running itself into the ground. Çağla Güleray and Furkan Güleray formed Ductape in 2019 in Istanbul, where their mix of post-punk, darkwave, Turkish and English lyrics quickly carried them well beyond the usual underground boundaries. Four albums and two EPs later, they have relocated their creative base to France. Geography changes; the unease travels well. On Faded Flowers, that unease has acquired a larger target. The title gives you the central image without turning it into homework: people as flowers left too long beneath bad light, drained by repetition, expectation, isolation, and the exhausting business of becoming whatever the surrounding machinery finds acceptable. You can hear that pressure everywhere. The basslines have the cold discipline of public transport at six in the morning. Synthesizers cut through with little sympathy. Furkan’s guitar keeps finding ways to sound agitated without becoming decorative, sometimes stalking around Çağla’s voice, sometimes answering it, sometimes scraping at the walls. Çağla’s magnificent voice remains the great destabilizing force in Ductape. She can sound detached enough to frighten you, then suddenly let some exposed nerve show through before the song has time to make a ceremony of it. There is very little comfort in that delivery, which suits an album concerned with the absurdity of living among millions of people and still feeling marooned. That particular contradiction runs all through Faded Flowers. Everyone is visible now. Everyone is reachable. Everyone is encouraged to construct a public version of themselves, polish it, post it, improve it, defend it, sell it, then wake up tomorrow and do the same miserable maintenance all over again. Somewhere along the line, identity became administrative labour. Ductape sounds thoroughly fed up with the arrangement. The album keeps circling the false authorities people submit to without necessarily believing in them: social roles, digital identities, manufactured ideals, systems of power, inherited expectations, all those little invisible rules that become oppressive mostly because nobody remembers agreeing to them. There is anger in these songs, but also exhaustion, and the exhaustion may be more interesting. Rage still assumes you have energy to spare. Fine considers one dubious convenience of hitting bottom: at least you can stop pretending the view is lovely. The album’s first single follows a collapse through pain and disorientation toward an unexpected sense of ownership, as Çağla finds a place for herself inside the very circumstances that have undone her. A steady bassline and luminous synthesizers carry her weary composure, giving that uneasy acceptance room to develop. There is something wonderfully suspect about feeling comfortable down there, and the song lets the suspicion sit beside the relief. Within an album preoccupied with keeping up appearances, surrendering the performance becomes its own small freedom. The accompanying black-and-white video turns that process into a homemade alchemical experiment. Filmed at Misuc in Ankara, it casts the duo as silent-film experimenters collecting ingredients and tending a potion among curious specimens. Ductape handled the direction, styling, and production, with camera work by Mert Yalçın and editing by Çağla Güleray. Its antique laboratory makes an apt workshop for two people attempting to assemble another version of themselves. Standout track Obscure moves with a bassline so blunt and heavy it seems capable of carrying the song by itself, while Furkan Güleray’s distorted guitar keeps worrying at the edges, leaving abrasions rather than decoration. Synths hang overhead with an icy, almost antiseptic quality, giving the music the uneasy stillness of a room where something unpleasant has already been said. Çağla Güleray sings in English, her low register remarkably composed as she picks through disillusionment without dressing it up for sympathy. That restraint makes the words hit harder. Stolen light, dead idols, resentment calcified through repetition, the dull vacancy that follows years of believing in something that eventually reveals itself as another instrument of control: Obscure gathers these ideas until the song begins to feel less like despair than the slow recognition of how thoroughly faith can be exploited. There is damage here, certainly, but also the uncomfortable clarity that comes when the old explanations have finally stopped working. Its Berlin performance video brings that severity onto the stage. Directed by Altay Erlik, with cinematography by Emrah Celik and laser animation by Peter Isachenko, the clip concentrates on the duo’s physical presence, giving the song’s accusations the directness of an encounter across a crowded room. On Gölgesiz, the effort of continuing becomes almost physical. Sung in Turkish, the album’s second single carries accumulated sorrow through persistent drums and guitar figures that seem caught in the same argument with themselves. Çağla keeps her delivery measured, making fatigue audible through the weight she gives each phrase. The rhythm maintains its appointment with the next bar while the person inside it struggles to find a reason to follow. That uneasy relationship between bodily momentum and emotional depletion gives the song its force, extending the album’s concern with lives organised around obligations that have outlasted their meaning. Made during Ductape’s Latin American tour, the monochrome DIY video places Çağla against expanses of water and open space, her figure often reduced to a silhouette. Visual distortions make her outline appear unstable, as though even occupying a body has become difficult work. The images give the song’s isolation a scale that the surrounding emptiness only enlarges. Faded Flowers gains its pull from the sense that decay is something social as much as personal. The individual breaks down because the surrounding structure is already cracked. The city keeps moving. The screen keeps glowing. The machine keeps asking for another password. Somewhere inside all that, a person still has to decide who they are. Ductape leave that question open, with the bass still moving underneath it. Listen to Faded Flowers below and order the album here. Faded Flowers by Ductape To celebrate the album release, Ductape have announced headline shows and festival dates across Europe well into 2027. items.body: John X Belmonte’s Golden Lore understands a basic truth about goth clubs, doomed romance, and every terrible decision made after midnight: grandeur works best when there is something embarrassing hiding underneath it. The song moves with the confidence of a man walking into a ruined cathedral wearing sunglasses, fully aware that vanity and remorse have been sharing the same coat for years. Its synth bass keeps the floor moving with a steady, narcotic insistence, while Belmonte’s voice sits low in the mix, deep and controlled, as though he is delivering private evidence to a room that has already reached its verdict. The pitch-shifted echo curling around the vocal gives Belmonte’s delivery a doubled quality, part confession and part apparition, suggesting memory as a badly behaved accomplice rather than some sacred archive. Golden Lore keeps circling myth, beauty, regret, and self-invention, those old poisons that people pour into prettier bottles whenever reality starts looking cheap. The lyrics seem fascinated by how easily memory turns vanity into legend, and how legend eventually gets mistaken for truth. Golden Lore belongs to that hour when the dance floor becomes less a public space than a private reckoning set to a bassline. Belmonte gives the song enough romantic scale to make regret feel almost luxurious, letting memory dress its worst decisions in expensive clothes. By the final chorus, desire, vanity, and remorse have become impossible to separate, and the song leaves them circling one another beneath the club lights until closing time. As a dance track, Golden Lore has excellent instincts. The rhythm remains disciplined, the bassline stays heavy, and every element serves the forward motion. Nothing gets cluttered for the sake of drama. Then the chorus opens up, and this is where the song earns its black clothes. The melody is gorgeous without becoming sugary, large without losing its bruised center. There is a real sense of release in the refrain, the kind that makes a crowded room briefly feel communal even when everyone inside it is busy maintaining their own private disaster. You can hear why fans of Cold Cave, Drab Majesty, Then Comes Silence, and the Sisters of Mercy might find an immediate point of entry, though Belmonte keeps enough restraint in the arrangement to avoid drowning the song in borrowed gestures. The video takes a similarly direct route. Belmonte performs against images of a mysterious figure moving through a dark landscape with a giant ankh, the superimposition giving the clip the look of damaged film discovered in somebody’s locked drawer. The imagery is simple, but it suits the song’s obsession with memory, myth, and the ghostly versions of ourselves we keep polishing. Watch the video for Golden Lore below: Based in New York City, John X Belmonte is an independent darkwave and post-punk artist drawn to the romantic and cinematic possibilities of gothic music. His work pairs brooding atmosphere with rhythmic urgency, giving beauty and emotional intensity equal room within its electronic arrangements. Released September 18, 2026, Golden Lore brings that sensibility to its examination of myth, memory, and remorse. Listen to Golden Lore on Spotify here. Follow John X.
